citation: Matuku & Kaseke (2014), 'The role of stokvels in improving people's lives: Orange Farm, Johannesburg', Social Work/Maatskaplike Werk
mechanisms: A stokvel works because it separates grocery money from other claims on irregular income, creating a disciplined buffer that smooths consumption across the year.
A burial society works because witnessing neighbours' funeral hardship turns shared vulnerability into a pooled response of equipment, labour and presence.
A rotating savings scheme works because small regular contributions are locked away from daily temptation, converting them into a lump sum that buys assets or pays large bills.

A stokvel works as a credit source because lending is confined mainly to a trusted circle, occasionally extending to trusted outsiders, where lender and borrower know each other's circumstances and social ties enforce repayment.
A stokvel spreads because visible uniforms and personal networks signal an accessible, socially endorsed institution with clear entry rules.
evaluative_rules: Earmark money for a specific purpose and keep it separate from daily spending — money that stays in the pocket gets absorbed.
Judge a financial arrangement by whether members carry each other in a crisis, not by what it pays back.
Value forced, collective discipline that turns small regular contributions into a lump sum for a deliberate purchase.
Borrow from and lend to people who know your circumstances and where you live; social ties are the real guarantee, not paperwork.
Trust what you see working in your own network — visible peers and clear entry rules count for more than any advertisement.
objection_patterns: Will the groceries I get match the money I put in?
Can I trust these people with my contributions?
Do I know where the borrowers live?
How do I join and what does it cost to enter?
confidence: qualitative case study, single township, fieldwork date not specified — mechanisms transferable, magnitudes unknown
